name: Grace Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for speaking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Clarke and Bell, a six-person ad agency on the ring road. Our biggest clients are car dealerships and a furniture chain, so my day is weekend sale ads, newspaper pages and big banners for showroom windows. Mr Clarke, the owner, writes the offers and I lay them out. I cut cars out of photos all day, which I've started doing with an AI tool because everyone else here does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy seeing my banner on the motorway billboard, my mum takes photos of it. What's difficult is that I'm still learning, and Hassan, our senior designer, redoes my headlines more often than I'd like. I'm patient, though. My dad always said you earn your place by turning up and getting better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always a new thing everybody gets excited about. I'd say hard work and good relationships with clients still matter most. I'd probably say that to the girls at choir and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my worry, car sales are, because dealerships cut the newspaper ads first and that's half my work. That happens every slow month. Mr Clarke has been talking about the furniture chain going online-only, which would hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and ask Hassan to teach me headlines properly. I'd keep saving, I've got about four months now. And I'd keep doing wedding invitations for people at church on weekends, which brings in a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not about robots, about whether the clients stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is the work at Clarke and Bell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes up and down with car sales. Last winter two dealerships cut their budgets and Mr Clarke didn't replace a designer who left. Nobody was let go, but nobody was hired either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you live with, and how does money work at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I share a flat with my cousin Ada, who's a nurse. We split the rent and the bills, and she's steadier than me because hospitals always need nurses. I send a little to my mum every month too, which I won't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business has to keep up, that's just how the market works. I'd say people should learn new skills instead of waiting for the government to fix it. I wouldn't post much, I'm private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is exactly what these tools do. A car dealer can type in the offer and the photo and get a weekend ad in a minute. Mr Clarke would keep Hassan for the big clients and I'd be the first one let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using more of the tools, once I'd seen Hassan get good results. I'd look at the in-house marketing jobs at Mayfield Motors, the dealership group, because a big firm moves slower and I already know their cars. And I'd save harder, an extra hundred a month, by cutting my clothes budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not someone who panics, but I can count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use one AI tool already. Would you use more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I'd seen them work. I'm not first in line for new things, but I'm not last either. If Hassan could do a full ad set in an hour with them, I'd learn it that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Clarke and Bell would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly me, honestly, and Lorraine at the front desk, who does the booking and the invoices. That's the kind of job these tools take on day one. She's been there twenty years and has a grandson she looks after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to pull together. I'd say the government should help businesses keep people working rather than hand out cheques. I'd mostly be praying, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Clarke and Bell is finished by 2028, and in-house jobs at Mayfield go too. Everything I do is on a screen, so robots coming later doesn't save me. I'd be out of work at twenty-eight or twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back to essentials straight away and push savings toward six months. I'd grow the wedding invitations into a proper small business, printed and posted, because people still want a card they can hold. And I'd look at hands-on work, maybe training as a dental nurse like my aunt, which gives me a few years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep a brave face at church and cry at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send money to your mum. What happens to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the last thing I'd cut, but it would get smaller. My mum would understand, she'd tell me to look after myself first. I'd feel like I'd failed her anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd go to family first, Ada and my uncles. Asking the government would feel like giving up, though I wouldn't judge anyone else for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning, so people should be sensible and learn something useful. Apprenticeships and real skills, not just more degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, design ends for me around 2030. Five years gives me time to build the invitation business and maybe train for something hands-on while I'm still paid. That's a lot better than two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the dental nurse course part-time and keep working at Clarke and Bell. I'd grow the invitations slowly, maybe a website. And I'd keep saving the extra hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can train while still paid, instead of scrambling. I'd be thirty-two with a new trade, which is young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, every day by then. I'd use them for the invitations too, so I could make more designs faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare. Work hard and plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, with ten years of experience and maybe a family. I'd still lose the design job, but I'd see it coming a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Clarke and Bell, keep saving and keep the invitations going. I'd wait two or three years to see if the tools really take over before training for something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace mostly. God gives us time for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years I can marry, maybe start a family and change careers, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting design college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to learn to work with people, not just screens. Design college is fine, but learn something with your hands too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to train for anything. What would help is paid apprenticeships in hands-on work, and help for small firms like Clarke and Bell to keep people on while they train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about my mum. My mum worked two jobs so I could go to design college, and I'd hate to tell her the diploma was for a job that doesn't exist.
